blocks.text: Rocks. A picturesque and wild spot. Dark night and complete solitude. Musical prelude. After a few moments a Smuggler appears on the summit of a rock, then another, then two, then twenty, descending and scrambling down the mass of rocks; some of them carrying heavy bales on their shoulders.
Carmen, Jose, Il Dancairo, Il Remendado, Frasquita, Mercedes, and Smuggler.

lines: Listen, comrades, listen!
Fortune waits below;
But of caution have we need,
Lest in a snare we fall.
This is a fine trade, but it needs
A strong heart when danger’s near,
Whether from above or below—what care we?
On we go, never showing fear,
Torrents braving, cliffs we scale
On the icy north-wind’s gale;
Storm and bullets we despise;
’Neath the coastguard’s watchful eyes
We bring our booty safe up here.
Listen, comrades, listen, etc.
Here let us rest awhile,—the night is dark,
And then forth will we go to discover
If the coast be clear,
And if without peril
The smugglers may proceed.

blocks.text: All stay excepting Il Dancairo and Il Remendado. During the scene between Carmen and Jose, some of the Gipsies light a fire, near which Frasquita and Mercedes seat themselves; the others, folding themselves in their mantles, lying down, go to sleep. Jose goes to the back, watching from the rocks.

lines: At what are you gazing?
I was thinking that in the world below
Dwells an aged good woman,
Who believes I am an honest man;
Alas! she is mistaken!
Whoever can she be?
Ah, Carmen! the thought is not difficult for her,—’tis my mother!
Well, you had better go to her this moment;
Indeed, the way of life here suits you not,
And you should be pleased to leave this place.
To go far from thee?
Certainly.
And leave thee, Carmen? I swear

blocks.text: Placing his hand on his knife.

lines: If thou sayst it again, ’twill be death!
This silence—to me reveals thy thoughts.
What matters it to me!
I shall die if fate wills it.

blocks.text: Turns her back on Jose, and goes to seat herself near Frasquita and Mercedes. After a moment’s hesitation, Jose also turns away and throws himself full length on the rocks. During Carmen’s last words, Mercedes and Frasquita draw out a pack of cards.

lines: Shuffle.
Throw.
Yes; so let it be.
Three cards for me.
Four to thee.
Declare to us, pretty cards,
What good the future will bring to me—
What will be—who will deceive us—
What sort of lovers we shall see.
Here I see a handsome lad,
Who to love me ever vows.
And I one who’s rich and old,
Who would fain make me his spouse.
I with him on his good steed
O’er the mountains far will ride.
To his castle the old knight
Bids me welcome—queen and bride,
With great love his heart o’erflows,
Ev’ry day brings us fresh joys.
I have all that I can wish,
Robes and rings and jewell’d toys.
Mine becomes a leader bold,
With him distant paths I tread.
And mine—no, no, he don’t last long—
Leaves me his money when he’s dead.
Speak again, speak, pretty cards,
What good the future will bring to me—
What will be—who will deceive us—
What sort of lovers shall we see
Money!
Love!

blocks.text: Carmen has watched the game throughout.

lines: Come, let me know my destiny.
Pictures! spades! a grave!
They lie not; first to me, and then to him,
And then to both—a grave!

blocks.text: In a low voice, continuing to shuffle the cards.

lines: In vain; to avoid the stern response
In vain I sort the cards;
’Twill nothing aid, the truth they declare,
They deceive not.
If in the book the page is clear,
Fear not; throw, and play.
The cards in thy hand will, if sorted rightly,
Pleasure to thee foretell;
But if thou must die, if the word so dread
Already in heaven is decreed,
The cards, to whose will thou art forced to yield,
Will again repeat thy doom.
Well, be it so; death must come!
Carmen will defy it! Carmen is strong!
Speak again, speak, pretty cards, &c.

blocks.text: Enter Il Dancairo and Il Remendado.

lines: What news!
We shall try to cross, and shall succeed.
Jose, stay here and watch the bales.
Is the path clear?
Yes, but there’s risk enough. Over the ravine
Where we must cross,
Three coastguards stand!—they must die!
Take up the bales, and away!
’Tis no use talking; pass you must.
The coastguard will be our affair:—
They like amusement, like other men,
And to play the gallant are willing.
Leave it to us the road to clear.
The coastguard will be very kind.
To us very humble they’ll be.
Yes, they’ll receive us graciously.
Our affair let the coastguard be:—
They like amusement, like other men,
And whilst the gallant with us they play,
Leave it to us your road to clear.
Their affair will the coastguard be, &c.
No need prowess to display.
The only way with them must be
With caresses to be free,
And entice them loving words to hear.
Our affair will the coastguard be, &c.
If they wish a kiss to take,
We’ll not say no; they are welcome quite.
And we’ll hold them in play until the hour
When you with the bales have passed out of sight.
Our affair, &c.

blocks.text: All go. Jose the last; and he is examining the barrels of his gun. A man passes on the rocks above. It is a Guide.

lines: Here is the hidden abode of the smugglers,
And here shall I Jose see;
And the duty his mother has enjoined me,
Without fear I shall know how to fulfil.
I try not to own that I tremble,
But I know I’m a coward, altho’ bold I appear,
Ah! how can I ever call up my courage,
While horror and dread chill my sad heart with fear.
Here, in this savage retreat,
Sad and weary am I, alone and sore afraid.
Ah! heav’n! to thee I humbly pray now:
Protect thou me, and guide and aid!
I shall see the guilty creature,
Who by infernal arts doth sever
From his country, from his duty,
Him I loved—and shall love ever!
I may tremble at her beauty,
But her power affrights me not.
Strong, in my just cause confiding,
Heaven! I trust myself to thee.
Ah! to this poor heart give courage,
Protector! guide and aid now me!
But I am not deceiv’d; no, he is on yon rock.
Ah, come! ah, come, Jose!—
My heart fails me! What can I do?—
How attract him?
Ah! a shot! Heaven! my heart fails me!

blocks.text: Disappears behind the rocks. Escamillo appears at the same moment.

lines: Two inches higher
And it would have been all over with me.
Who art thou? Speak out.
Eh? Softly, softly, my lad:
I am Escamillo, Toreador of Granada.
Escamillo?
The same.
The name is known to me:
Thou art welcome, comrade;
But dost thou really mean to stay here?
I can tell thee—no.
But I have been touched in my heart, lad,
And he who is so, merits not being born
If he’ll not risk his life in search of his love.
The object of your love dwells here?
Yes, truly. A gipsy is she—charming;
What is her name?
Carmen.
Carmen?
She had a lover,
A dragoon, who became a deserter.
He loved her; she loved him;
But she is weary of him.
Carmen’s love does not last.
In spite of that, thou lovest her?
Yes, to desperation!
Hold! who will the zingara seduce,
Do not forget, will pay for it.
’Tis not difficult: thou art the deserter,
The handsome dragoon she loves—
Or rather that she did love.
I am.
I am pleased, and I know not how to deny it.

blocks.text: Both draw their knives, enveloping the left arm in their cloaks.

lines: At last my rage I can vent,
And this villain’s heart will I pierce.
My unlucky star is in the ascendant,
While seeking the fair one, the rival I’ve met.
Out with thy blade, and keep at bay:
Neither will quarter give;
’Tis agreed one must fall.
Nor he nor I shall live.

blocks.text: Put themselves in fighting positions. Carmen arrives with Dancairo, and stays Jose’s arm as he is about to strike Escamillo. Il Remendado, Mercedes, Frasquita and Gipsies rush in.

lines: Jose, hold!
’Tis well. And with great joy
I see that to thee, Carmen, my life I owe.
As to thee, my gay dragoon,
I am at thy service, and we will again,
Any day thou wishest, try our fortunes.
We shall see thee again, then.
Now we are ready to depart, and thou—
Good-bye, lad!
’Tis at least allowed me, since leave I must,
To invite you all to the bull-fight at Seville;
I hope there to shine;
And whoever loves me will come.
Dragoon, don’t be angry.
I go, then; perhaps we shall one day meet.

blocks.text: Jose tries to rush at the Toreador. Il Dancairo and Il Remendado prevent him. Escamillo goes out leisurely.

lines: Ah! Carmen, beware!
I am weary of suffering.

blocks.text: Carmen shrugs her shoulders, and moves away from him.

lines: Come! it is agreed we leave.
Yes, yes, we must depart.
Look above! some one vainly tries to hide.

blocks.text: Goes to see, and brings in Michaela.

lines: A woman!
By heaven! a pleasant surprise!
Michaela!
Don Jose!
Unfortunate girl!
What doest thou in this place?
In search of thee I came.
In her cot in the far off valley.
Prays thy mother, unhappy man!
Weeps till my heart bleeds,
Weeps and waits for thee ever;
Return to her; hasten, Jose.
Ah, with me now come!
Go, and go quickly; stay not here;
This way of life is not for thee.
To depart thou dost counsel me?
Yes, thou shouldst go—
That thou mayst follow
Another lover—the toreador.
No, on my honor, no!
I’ll rather die!—all may hear me.
No, Carmen, I will not depart;
And the tie that binds us
I will not free thee from.
Be not deaf to my prayers;
Thy mother waits thee there.
The chain that binds thee, Jose,
Death will break.
To my counsel yield thee;
No, Jose, stay not here.
The chain that binds thee,
Death alone can break.
Go from hence;
I cannot follow thee.
Mine thou art, accursed one!
And I will force thee to know
And submit to the fate
That both our lives unites.
Yet one word—’twill be my last:—
Thy mother’s dying!
Thou wilt not that she leaves the world
Ere she has pardoned thee?
My mother dying?
Yes, Don Jose.
Let us this moment depart.
Be satisfied—I quit you;
But we shall meet again.

blocks.text: Going away with Michaela. The Toreador’s voice is heard in the distance.

lines: Toreador, e’er watchful be;
Do not forget the brightest of eyes
Are fondly thee waiting,
And love is the prize.

blocks.text: Jose stops at the back, on the rocks. He hesitates, but decides at last, and goes on his way with Michaela. Carmen, leaning on a large stone, watches his departure. The Gipsies take up their bales and proceed on their journey.
